content.title: How long have the Starliner astronauts been in space? Not as long as these 5 spacefarers.
content.text: NASA astronauts Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams are potentially days away from heading back to Earth and putting the whole Boeing Starliner debacle behind them for good.In less than a week, the experienced spacefarers could be boarding a SpaceX Dragon capsule with the Crew-9 mission team and undocking from the International Space Station for a water landing in Florida. The imminent homecoming would be a poignant moment for Wilmore and Williams, who never expected to live and work at the orbital laboratory for more than nine months when they arrived back in June.The week-or-so the crew of the ill-fated Starliner spacecraft were meant to be at the space station has now stretched into the better part of a year – far surpassing the length of the majority of orbital missions. But it's also not unheard of for NASA astronauts to remain in space for longer than 200 days.That's a milestone Williams and Wilmore hit long ago, but NASA and SpaceX are working to ensure they don't join the rare 300-day club.If all goes to plan – and as Wednesday's delayed SpaceX launch proved, that's always a question mark – the mission to set the stage for the Starliner astronauts to return to Earth could be getting off the ground Friday night. That would make Williams and Wilmore's spaceflight the sixth longest in NASA history.Here's a look at how long the Startlier crew has been at the space station, and the five NASA astronauts who have spent even more consecutive days in space.Starliner saga: As Starliner astronauts prepare for return, look back at the mission's biggest momentsNASA astronauts Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams walk June 1 at NASA's Kennedy Space Center. The experienced astronauts ended up launching June 5 on the Boeing's Starliner's first crewed flight test mission.How many days have Suni Williams, Butch Wilmore been in space?As of Friday, Williams and Wilmore have spent 281 days at the International Space Station.The astronauts, who are both on their third trip to orbit, were selected to pilot the Boeing Starliner for its first crewed spaceflight in June.Boeing had been developing the vehicle to join SpaceX's Dragon as a second operational spacecraft for NASA under the space agency's commercial crew program. The program allows NASA to pay commercial companies to launch and transport astronauts and cargo to orbit aboard their own vehicles, freeing up NASA to focus on its Artemis lunar program and other deep space missions, including future crewed expeditions to Mars.But Boeing's Starliner spacecraft was plagued by a slew of helium leaks and propulsion issues when it reached the space station with its crew. After months of deliberations, NASA officials decided to send the Starliner back to Earth in September without Williams and Wilmore.NASA and SpaceX then launched the Crew-9 mission later that same month with two astronauts instead of four, leaving two seats on a Dragon spacecraft reserved for Wilmore and Williams for the return journey. The Starliner crew members have also joined the station's Expedition 72, which Williams commands.What NASA astronauts have had longer duration missions than Starliner Crew?If the Crew-9 team departs as scheduled, Williams and Wilmore will have ended their stint with 286 consecutive days in orbit – just shy of NASA astronaut Peggy Whitson's 289-day mission between November 2016 and September 2017.Whitson is among the only five NASA astronauts who have ever spent more consecutive days in orbit than Wilmore and Williams.Those five are:Frank Rubio, who spent 371 days in orbit in 2022-23, the longest single spaceflight by a U.S. astronaut in history;Scott Kelly, who in March 2015 launched on a 340-day mission in space;Christina Koch, whose 328-day-long mission between March 2019 and February 2020 helped her set a record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman;Peggy Whitston, who spent 289 consecutive days in space and is NASA's record-holder for most cumulative days in orbit, with 675 total days in space since 2002.Frank Rubio's record-setting spaceflight was similar to the Starliner caseInternational Space Station (ISS) crew member and NASA astronaut Frank Rubio reacts while sitting in a chair shortly after landing in the Soyuz MS-23 space capsule in a remote area near Zhezkazgan, Kazakhstan, Sept. 27, 2023.Astronaut Frank Rubio etched his name in the history books in September 2023 when his 371 days in orbit made him the American with the record for the longest spaceflight.But it was a record that Rubio, then-47, never expected to break when he and two cosmonauts launched Sept. 21, 2022 from a site in Kazakhstan. Rather, Rubio and crew thought they'd return to Earth the following March after just six months.And the culprit behind the crew's unanticipated extended stay? Just like for the Starliner crew, it was trouble with same capsule meant to ferry them back to Earth.When the Russian Soyuz capsule sprang a coolant leak in 2022 after it was pierced by a piece of space junk, a new spacecraft was rushed to the orbital outpost so the stranded spacefarers could make it back to Earth. Rubio's time in space came to an end Sept. 27 when the Army doctor and helicopter pilot landed with the Russians in a remote area of Kazakhstan in the replacement Soyuz that had only reached them two weeks prior.How long are astronauts typically at the International Space Station?Astronauts with missions aboard the International Space Station are generally gone for about six months, putting Wilmore and Williams among rare company, according to NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.Designed and operated thanks to a global partnership of space agencies, the International Space Station has been home to crews of astronauts, cosmonauts and plenty of others since November 2000, NASA says. While there, the spacefarers spend their time conducting a variety of scientific experiments while doing work to maintain and improve the station's operations.Seven spacefarers are currently at the station, including four Americans and three Russians.When could the Starliner astronauts return home?The astronauts of NASA and SpaceX's joint Crew 10 mission, (from left) Kirill Peskov, Nichole Ayers, Takuya Onishi and Anne McClain, prepare for launch Wednesday at the Kennedy Space Center before the voyage to the International Space Station was delayed.Before Starliner astronauts Wilmore and Williams can depart the station with Crew-9, they must await the arrival of the mission's successors.The mission known as Crew-10, jointly operated by NASA and SpaceX, had been due to get off the ground Wednesday night from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The launch was called off due to an issue with the launchpad’s ground system and has since been rescheduled for Friday night.If that happens, a Dragon capsule carrying NASA astronauts Anne McClain and Nichole Ayers, along with Japanese astronaut Takuya Onishi of the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) and Roscosmos cosmonaut Kirill Peskov could arrive Saturday night at the station.Once docked, Ayers, McClain, Onishi and Peskov will spend a few days becoming familiarized with their new home and the work taking place during a handover period.Williams, Wilmore and the rest of Crew-9 – NASA astronaut Nick Hague and Roscosmos cosmonaut Aleksandr Gorbunov – could then depart no earlier than Wednesday, March 19 for a splashdown landing off the Florida coast.Eric Lagatta covers breaking and trending news for USA TODAY. Reach him at elagatta@gannett.comThis article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Starliner astronauts have 280 days in space: These 5 spent longer
